chapters.title: Chapter 3: Gold as a Macro Hedge

lessons.title: Building Gold Exposure in an Indian Portfolio: SGBs, ETFs, and Physical Gold

children.text: Four Ways to Own Gold, Four Different Cost Structures

Now that you understand why gold moves, real rates, the dollar, central banks and cultural demand, the practical question is which wrapper to hold it in. India offers four genuinely different routes: physical gold, gold ETFs, gold fund of funds, and Sovereign Gold Bonds. They are not interchangeable. Each carries a different cost structure, a different liquidity profile, and a different tax outcome, and the right choice depends far more on your holding period than on which one 'performs best', since all four ultimately track the same underlying gold price.

body.text: The best gold instrument is not the one with the best historical return. All four track the same gold price. The best one is whichever has costs and liquidity that actually match how long you intend to hold it.

children.text: Physical Gold: The Instrument With the Highest Hidden Costs

Physical gold is culturally the default in India, but it is the most expensive way to hold it as an investment. Making charges on jewellery, which can run well into double digits as a percentage of the gold's value, are rarely recovered when you sell, since resale value is based mainly on the gold content, not the craftsmanship you paid for. Since June 2021, BIS hallmarking with a unique HUID number has become mandatory for jewellers selling hallmarked gold, which meaningfully reduces, though does not eliminate, purity risk if you buy from a compliant seller.

body.label: GST on Gold Purchase
body.value: 3% on gold value, 5% on making charges
body.context: This has been the standard GST structure on gold jewellery since GST's introduction in July 2017. It applies on top of the price of the gold itself and adds directly to your cost basis.

children.text: Gold ETFs and Fund of Funds: The Convenience Route

A gold ETF holds physical gold in an audited vault and issues units that trade on the exchange, so buying one through a broker like Zerodha is functionally identical to buying a share. If you do not have a demat account, or want to run a monthly SIP the way you would into an equity fund, a gold fund of funds invests in an underlying gold ETF on your behalf, at the cost of one extra layer of expense on top of the ETF's own.
Sovereign Gold Bonds: Built for a Fixed Horizon

SGBs, introduced in Chapter 1, run on an eight-year tenor from issue, with the RBI opening early redemption windows on specific interest payment dates from the fifth year onward. If you sell earlier on the exchange instead of waiting for those windows or maturity, you get market liquidity, but typically thinner trading volumes than a gold ETF, and you give up the tax exemption that only applies to holding through to maturity. This makes SGBs a strong fit for a goal with a known, multi-year horizon, and a poor fit if you might need to exit on short notice.

body.text: Capital gains tax rules for gold ETFs and gold mutual funds changed in April 2023 and were revised again under the new capital gains framework introduced in the July 2024 Budget. Because these rules have shifted twice in quick succession, check the current holding-period and rate rules with a tax advisor or the latest Income Tax Act provisions rather than relying on a specific rate from this or any other course.

Digital gold, sold through payment apps in partnership with providers like MMTC-PAMP or SafeGold, sits in a regulatory grey zone. It is not regulated by SEBI as a security or by the RBI as a deposit, and buyers rely entirely on the platform's own custodian arrangements. This gap has drawn caution from regulators, and it is worth understanding that digital gold does not carry the same regulatory protections as an exchange-listed ETF or an RBI-issued bond.

body.title: Match the Instrument to the Goal
body.scenario: An investor wants to build a gold position today for a child's wedding exactly eight years from now. They are comfortable locking the money away for the full period and want to minimise cost and maximise the after-tax outcome, and liquidity before the eight years are up is not a concern.
body.prompt: Which of the four instruments best fits this specific goal, and why?
body.modelAnswer: A Sovereign Gold Bond is the strongest fit. The eight-year investment horizon lines up exactly with the SGB's tenor, so the illiquidity that makes SGBs a poor choice for short-notice needs is irrelevant here. Holding to maturity means the investor earns the fixed 2.5% annual interest on top of the gold price move, and the capital gains at maturity are tax-exempt for individual holders, an advantage no ETF, fund of funds, or physical gold purchase can match. Since new issuance may not always be open, the investor should also check whether buying existing SGBs on the secondary market, which still offers the same maturity-linked tax treatment, is a practical alternative.

points: All four gold instruments track the same underlying price. The right choice depends on your holding period and need for liquidity, not on which one you expect to 'outperform'.
Physical gold carries the highest hidden costs, mainly making charges that are rarely recovered on resale, and purity risk unless the piece is BIS hallmarked with a HUID.
Gold ETFs and gold fund of funds offer the most convenient, liquid, buy-and-hold exposure, with the FoF route available to investors without a demat account.

Sovereign Gold Bonds are built for a fixed, multi-year horizon: the tax exemption and 2.5% interest reward holding to maturity, and only make sense if your goal's timeline actually matches the bond's tenor.

Gold's capital gains tax treatment has changed twice in recent years, so verify the current rules before assuming any specific rate, and treat digital gold's lack of formal regulatory protection as a real, not theoretical, consideration.
